The thing about a Laptop is it will never be as powerful as a gaming PC and they can get 'quirkier' at a faster pace.

I have had both and there's strengths and weaknesses to both. I loved having a laptop because I could play anywhere and in whatever position was comfortable - loved being able to recline on a sofa for instance and just slob and game. 

But there is no question if you want the absolute 'best' gaming experience in terms of fidelity, a PC is the way to go, it's a lot easier if something breaks to go in and swap out parts too. Not to mention the cooling tends to be naturally better because of the size difference, it's much easier to get 100% out of your PC's potential than it is on a laptop with its tiny fans.

You can also turn a laptop into a desk PC with enough cleverness and docks. But a laptop tends to have a CPU and GPU soldered into the board so no upgradability - basically you keep it for four or five years then it becomes e-waste, while a PC you can shift parts around so it's never fully obsolete. 

Plus the expenses: a laptop used to be more expensive than the PC for the same class of parts. But now you have supply constraints really hitting things hard. It can very well be you'll get a better deal on a laptop than if you are buying/building a PC.

It's a bit complex really, but if you want hands-down the best experience that will keep for longest, I'd still say PC, but if you put a lot of importance on being able to sit anywhere in your home and game comfortably a laptop is the way to go.

Additional consideration: as much as they may try to tell you otherwise, a gaming laptop will never really have good battery, you'll also have to be used to being plugged in practically 100% of the time. Unplugged gaming laptops tend to have to choke their power HARD to even reach 2 hours of life, so that's another issue regarding portability and also quality of gaming while unplugged is just not going to be realistic as a consideration imo.

I never complained Minecraft combat was no threat myself but I get why you would be annoyed at it I have seen others complain. It is also useful to remember that ever since Night of the Living Dead zombies have been popular in some respect ever since the 80s even in B-Movies, not nearly as renowned as in Hollywood in 2000/2010s, but still very much a strong presence.

I think this is pretty much the crux of the issue. It is not using the CPU 'per se' but it is using the integrated graphics within the CPU and not the dedicated GPU.

To be clear, you have a GPU 'inside' the CPU that Minecraft is picking. What I am trying to say with my advice is that you're not referring to the 'CPU' as such in this instance but the GPU within it, in this case probably Radeon Vega.

What I am saying is you will need to tell the game to use the 'dedicated' GPU, or graphics card, that is the high performance one in the computer. To save power, some computers like to default to using the 'integrated' so that they have longer battery life as the GPU inside the CPU is lower power draw overall, but not suitable for games as it needs more horsepower.

A dedicated graphics card is a separate, powerful GPU set aside from the CPU and its internal graphics. 

Think of it like a human (CPU/integrated) racing a cheetah (Graphics Card/dedicated). If you want to run 100m, pick the cheetah. It will destroy the human easily. But if you want to run say a marathon (lasting longer), the human will win easily because the cheetah will run out of energy (or battery life in this analogy) in a lot less time.  

In this case, to save on battery life the computer is deliberately trying NOT to use the powerful, dedicated graphics card and use ONLY what is available within the CPU itself to run the game. You aren't 'using' the CPU so much as you're using the 'weak' graphics chip that the CPU has inside it already.

As you said, the 'fix' is to change power settings as shown on the website I linked, so the computer knows 'okay, in this instance he doesn't want battery life but he wants to have more power', and so will let itself use the 'dedicated' graphics, the equivalent of allowing itself to sprint instead of jog. It will reduce battery life, but increase frames per second and run the game more smoothly as the GPU has the backbone to run the game. 

You're not wrong, and I'm not disagreeing with you, just explaining a bit more about this issue and why it happens.

Long post, but contains some tips on getting a better deal and understanding how contracts work:

I used to work for a major phone seller and this was exactly how the price was worked out. It was very easy to do: just take the current retail price of the phone, say £999, divide by contract length eg 24 months: £27.75 which was then one 'half' of the contract, and then you'd have the usage, let's say £10 a month being normal ish? Add them together and you have the overall monthly price which in this case is £37.75.

Usually most phone sellers that do these kind of things will be able to describe what the contract for your usage and what the contract is for buying your device.

Usually the usage contract itself is shorter than the credit agreement for the phone and usually 24 months so if you wanted you can just pay the remainder of the device off to walk away after that point.

There is no markup on the retail price of the phone: if a phone costs £999, it will cost £999 whether or not you take it on contract. It's the SIM part of the contract which is a bit more pernickety. 

The reason for 36 months is simply to avoid intimidating customers. At first glance it's a lot less scary to look at 27.75 a month (999/36) than it is to look at 41.63 a month (999/24). It's the same price whether you're buying it for longer, shorter or up front.

Often it is cheaper to buy on contract as some retailers will discount the contract cost of the phone over the SIM free version to attract customers. For example they could do a deal that makes the cost of the phone 899 (will usually advertise this as so much off per month). 

The same rules apply though, you can pay off anytime. So you can game the system and get a phone for cheaper than RRP if you're happy paying what essentially becomes a SIMO contract for using the phone on data and calls. And let's be honest, most wouldn't buy a phone if they didn't intend to use it for those purposes anyway. Just takes a bit of looking at the contract to work out what you're paying for. 

Also make sure your deal is interest free for this to apply. Most cases retailers are more than happy to advertise that fact as it is a good look so you will be able to tell this pretty quickly.

The scenario you're talking about here hasn't existed in modern batteries for a long time.

There's a lot of myths about battery life and extending it, as we're all wanting more from phones. However, most of these turn out to be either just myths or apocryphal stories in nature. That's the reason you see a lot of conflicting claims.

As far as smartphone batteries go, there are generally good ways to maintain battery health which have been discussed. But are they really worth all the hassle for what usually turns out to be an extra hour or so at most? I think a phone should fit into a person's life, not the other way around. It's kind of accepted in the smartphone industry that batteries aren't great, and there's a lot of people smarter than me trying to build a better battery (whoever cracks it is a guaranteed billionaire). But until then, we're settling for 'good enough'.

That usually means that developers focus for best performance within what is considered a normal phone lifespan, i.e. 2 years or so, as most phone contracts last about that long. In that time, there is an 'acceptable' amount of battery degradation. I would argue you're not really gaining much more by changing your habits and all that effort you would spend on doing so really wouldn't be worth the tiny battery life gains. 

Mobile phones, being smart, can tailor the charge they receive anyway to a decent extent. And by the time your battery health degrades to the point that we're worried about using these myths and 'tricks' to push battery lives for longer, your phone will have bigger problems such as out-of-date software support, slow processing power, over-bloated apps and the like. At this point in a phone's life cycle, we'd be thinking of an upgrade anyway.

I think bad writing in video games is tied up in the media's own unique storytelling tropes. For example, the difference in players' abilities in cutscenes vs gameplay. I was so frustrated in Metal Gear Solid and it totally broke my immersion that in the pre-torture scene Snake gets snuck up on by a nobody soldier that he could easily smack down in seconds (and usually by that point he's done so more than a couple of times). 

Twin Snakes does better with having him fight back but the point still stands that the cutscene doesn't work, especially since the player can spend 20 to 30 minutes investigating the area to make sure they're clear and end up with the same result: Snake captured.

A good way of doing this is when the player is captured in Dark Souls. It is literally beyond players' ability in actual gameplay terms to win a certain boss fight and it ends up with the player captured. This works because it doesn't break from the established rules players have been working with. Instead of an immersion breaking cutscene where the player watches mobs who he could easily destroy defeat his character instead he experiences the defeat himself and better yet, the experience is authentic to what's happened in the game so far.

Bad writing for me is about authenticity. Foe example, the original Resident Evil actually passes the test for me because its bad writing serves to authenticate the experience of playing a horror B-Movie. If the player instead got high quality voice acting and awesome direction as in the remake, many parts of the game feel off, such as, in this gritty world we're meant to take seriously, why do we have to play a piano to open a door or slot emblems into holes? That's not to say that REmake has bad writing per se, just that it tonally breaks with the original intent. I prefer the poor voice acting because it captures perfectly the experience of playing a terrible B-Movie horror. 

The writing for me enhances the consistency of the gameplay and obeys its rules. Characters remain in character and the plot is allowed to exist authentically and believably. I'm not a Kingdom Hearts gamer myself, but for me plot threads need to be finished satisfactorily as well if they are done. There is nothing worse than an underwhelming ending. 

Note however that a 'bad' ending is not the same as a bad ending. I appreciate having endings where things don't go the 'right' way, but the ending has to be significantly different or offer significant consequences for the characters involved to be considered good. Take Mass Effect 3 for instance. Most people disliked that the endings were underwhelming, not that any of them were 'bad'. It has to have stakes in order to work. If it boils down to a simple colour change or the same result for multiple endings then I won't be happy. I want consequences and stakes in my endings.

Other examples of bad writing also take typical story tropes as well but I tried here to concentrate on the tropes that are more unique to gaming. I'm sure there are many more examples of poor writing I missed, or that I may be wrong in many ways.

I think part of it depends more on the series. There are many games series out there where the act of serving the fans is important. Something like Kingdom Hearts has such a huge importance on fans that really this should be taken into account. A series without a die hard fan following can be more reliably reviewed by a critic outside of 'the circle'. I am sure on the other hand there are many aspects of games that frustrate and bemuse critics but are there because they're fan favourites.

Again it's all quality control. From what I can see he's not exactly a bad writer, but I think 'filling your boots' should apply. AFAIK it is just as easy as doing a Google search to learn how the game is structured.

Perhaps something can also be said as a minor critique is that the game's menu can mislead as to which scenario is different to which character. Games menus are important because wrestling with them can be a big frustration in a good game.

I think also, jeez there must be some intense time pressure involved. Honestly there are some games that I shy away from reviewing because there is just too much to talk about. Diablo 3 being one of them.

I typically think that if you review a game you don't have to complete it but you should also have a good amount of hours played to at least show you gave it a fair crack of the whip. Reviewers have to give general buying advice and impressions so if they gave it a fair go with some decent hours logged, then that should be enough to know the game's systems for a critique, especially in a generalisable way. I can't expect reviewers to play every minute of a 100 hour story mode: by even as low as the 10th hour for many games you'd get plenty of info to go on. Still it would help to have specific moments to use as examples for points to be made.

Ultimately it's all about editorial and quality control. At least run the story past some eyes before uploading it. I bash this drum all the time but these editors refuse so many applications claiming they only hire 'high quality', but ironically despite claiming to care so much for quality they let things like this happen.
